story.title: A Striped Cloak and a Celestial Globe: When Two Dutch Envoys Met Imam Sultan bin Saif in 1672 Muscat

story.meta_description: Preserved in The Hague, 1672 Dutch VOC dispatches reveal an eyewitness portrait of Imam Sultan bin Saif Al Ya'rubi, Amsterdam astronomy, and Muscat's global port.

detail.extracted_title: A Striped Cloak and a Celestial Globe: When Two Dutch Envoys Met Imam Sultan bin Saif in 1672 Muscat
detail.excerpt: Preserved for three centuries in The Hague, two eyewitness dispatches capture an ailing Ya'rubi Imam who dressed like an ordinary citizen, debated Amsterdam astronomy, and rode through the night to defend Muscat.
detail.article_html:
On 28 June 1672, inside a residence in Muscat, two representatives of the Dutch East India Company stepped into the presence of Imam Sultan bin Saif I Al Ya'rubi, the ruler whose forces had driven the Portuguese out of Muscat twenty-two years earlier and turned Oman into a formidable maritime power across the western Indian Ocean.

Expecting the gilded distance typical of seventeenth-century courts, the envoys—physician-diplomat Robert Padbrugge and Bandar Abbas company official Georg Wilmson—found something altogether different. Though visibly weakened by severe illness, the Imam welcomed the European visitors with warm composure. At his waist hung a scabbard and hilt inlaid with silver, and atop his head sat a fine white turban with a loose end falling roughly sixty-five centimeters. Yet his outer sleeveless cloak, woven in dark grey wool with crisp white bands spaced a hand's width apart, was indistinguishable from the everyday cloaks worn by ordinary Omani men in the streets outside.

Three and a half centuries later, the surviving Dutch dispatches from that June mission—preserved in the National Archives in The Hague and published in Arabic translation within Sheikh Dr. Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi's documentary collection Majma' Al-Tawarikh li-Shibh Al-Jazira Al-Arabiya wa Faris (1622–1810), recently examined by Omani historian Dr. Ahlam bint Hamoud Al Jahwari—offer a rare external portrait of Ya'rubi Oman at the height of its early sovereignty.

Why Diplomacy Stalled Between Trade and Defense

By 1672, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) had spent nearly eight years courting Muscat. Beginning in 1664, VOC directors sought permission to open a permanent agency in the port and secure customs privileges along Oman's busy sea lanes.

Yet when Padbrugge and Wilmson sat down with Omani officials in June 1672, the two sides were negotiating for fundamentally different prizes. Fresh from liberating Muscat in 1650 and determined to pursue Portuguese fleets across the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, the Omanis insisted that any pact include active military cooperation against Lisbon's strongholds. Bound by a European peace treaty with Portugal and anxious to avoid antagonizing rival European crowns, the Dutch envoys had orders to sign nothing beyond a commercial trade accord.

Neither side yielded its strategic red line, and formal treaty talks ended without a signature. Paradoxically, that diplomatic deadlock produced two remarkably candid historical records: Padbrugge's 121-page account dispatched from Colombo on 1 September 1672 to Ceylon Governor Rijckloff van Goens, and Wilmson's 11-page report sent on 2 February 1674 to Bandar Abbas director François de Haze.

Amsterdam Astronomy and a Night Ride From Nizwa

What lingers most vividly in Padbrugge's Colombo dispatch is not commercial bookkeeping, but human observation. A trained man of medicine and science who died in 1703, Padbrugge recorded the physical strength and upright bearing of Omani men, noting their courteous, generous conduct toward one another and toward foreign guests alike, alongside an outspoken admiration for courage and moral character.

During their audience, conversation turned unexpectedly from maritime politics to the stars. Imam Sultan bin Saif showed keen curiosity about astronomical instruments, engaging Padbrugge in a discussion of a mechanical celestial globe—moved slowly by delicate threads—newly invented in Amsterdam by the celebrated Dutch cartographer Joan Blaeu. Even amid constant naval vigilance, Muscat's leadership kept an attentive eye on global scientific invention.

Wilmson's 1674 report captures the equally relentless pace of the Imam's defense of the coast. After waiting at length in Muscat for an audience, the Dutch party rode inland toward Nizwa through punishing summer terrain where scarce water forced travelers to ration every skin. Two days along the mountain track, word reached their camp that Imam Sultan bin Saif had ridden right past them in the dark—hurrying straight back toward Muscat after intelligence arrived of a threatened Portuguese strike on the harbor. Compelled to turn their exhausted mounts around through the rocky wadis, the envoys reached Muscat the next day to find the Imam already back at his court.

Muscat's Harbor Ledger Across Ten Seas

Before departing, Wilmson compiled detailed shipping counts of the vessels dropping anchor in Muscat—a ledger that explains why European companies were so eager for a foothold there in the first place. Under Ya'rubi protection, ships converged on Muscat from the coasts of India and Sindh, the Maldives, the Malay Archipelago, East Africa, Mocha, Aden, Bahrain, Qatar, and Al-Ahsa.

Written not by court chroniclers seeking praise, but by frustrated foreign negotiators reporting home to Colombo and Bandar Abbas, the 1672 papers preserve an unvarnished glimpse of Oman's character: an Imam dressed like his own citizens, curious about the movement of the heavens, and ready to ride through the night whenever Muscat's coastline called.

detail.instagram_caption:
On 28 June 1672, two Dutch East India Company envoys—physician Robert Padbrugge and company official Georg Wilmson—stepped into a Muscat audience with Imam Sultan bin Saif I Al Ya'rubi, twenty-two years after Omani forces had expelled the Portuguese from the harbor.

Preserved for three and a half centuries in the National Archives in The Hague, their dispatches capture details no domestic chronicle thought to record. Though suffering from severe illness, the Imam greeted his European visitors warmly while wearing a dark grey sleeveless cloak woven with white stripes—identical to the everyday cloaks worn by ordinary Omani citizens. Between tough negotiations over maritime alliances, he questioned Padbrugge intently about a mechanical, thread-driven celestial globe newly invented in Amsterdam by cartographer Joan Blaeu.

Days earlier, when rumors of a Portuguese raid reached the interior, the Imam had ridden silently through the night from the Nizwa road straight back to defend Muscat, passing the Dutch caravan in the dark over rugged mountain wadis—while ships from India, Sindh, the Maldives, the Malay Archipelago, East Africa, Mocha, Aden, and the Gulf crowded his port.
